power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Importance: Firearm violence is an important public health problem in the US.
Timely identification and intervention for people who have thoughts of shooting others may help reduce the risk of firearm violence.
Objective: To examine the psychological and behavioral characteristics associated with thoughts of shooting others.
Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional analyses of the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide (NFACS) survey administered from May 27 to September 2, 2025.
The sample included 7034 US adults aged 18 years or older.
Survey weights were used to align the sample to national population benchmarks.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Lifetime and past-12-month thoughts of shooting others.

Correlates included self-reported offensive and defensive gun use, firearm experience and substance-involved firearm handling, firearm-and non-firearm-related victimization, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, psychiatric and substance use problems, antisocial behavior, and personality.

Results: Respondents who endorsed lifetime thoughts of shooting others (7.3% lifetime, n = 516; 3.3% past 12 months, n = 231) had higher rates of self-reported offensive (aOR = 3.38; 95% CI, 2.29-5.00) and defensive gun use (aOR = 3.60; 95% CI, 2.67-4.85), firearm and nonfirearm victimization, handling or firing a gun under the influence of alcohol or drugs, insecure firearm storage (i.e., unlocked and loaded), and more experience with firearms.
Thoughts of firearm suicide were strongly associated with thoughts of shooting others (lifetime aOR = 6.24; 95% CI, 4.57-8.51; past 12 months aOR = 9.25; 95% CI, 5.33-16.06).
Thoughts of shooting others were also associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors broadly and depression, anxiety, and substance use problems.
Respondents who reported thoughts of shooting others also reported high levels of antisocial behavior, intimate partner violence, and disinhibited personality traits.

Conclusions and Relevance: Characteristics associated with thoughts of shooting others include risk factors across multiple domains, similar to those associated with firearm and nonfirearm interpersonal violence and victimization.

Future research should examine whether a combination of screening for thoughts of shooting others and assessment of associated risk factors can improve risk formulation and inform prevention strategies for firearm violence.
Firearm violence remains a serious public health problem in the US with nearly 140,000 intentional shootings, including almost 18,000 homicides in 2023 1,2 .
Many more people, however, have seriously thought about shooting others.
A recent national survey found that 7.3% of US adults have thought about shooting another person in their lifetime and 3.3% have thought about shooting someone in the past 12 months 3 .
text.formatted: A recent national survey found that 7.3% of US adults have thought about shooting another person in their lifetime and 3.3% have thought about shooting someone in the past 12 months <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref> .

text.text: While most people will not act on these thoughts, some do, and so those who have thoughts of shooting others are an important and poorly understood risk group who warrant further study for gun violence prevention efforts.
In demographic terms, thoughts of shooting others were associated with younger age, male sex, Black compared to White respondents, living in an urban area, and lower income and education 3 .
text.formatted: In demographic terms, thoughts of shooting others were associated with younger age, male sex, Black compared to White respondents, living in an urban area, and lower income and education <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref> .

text.text: These associations are consistent with the demographic correlates of firearm interpersonal violence and victimization [4] [5] [6] , suggesting that assessing thoughts of shooting others may be effective in identifying a high-risk group.
text.formatted: These associations are consistent with the demographic correlates of firearm interpersonal violence and victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[6]</ref> , suggesting that assessing thoughts of shooting others may be effective in identifying a high-risk group.

text.text: Interestingly, thoughts of shooting others were not associated with current gun ownership, indicating that despite having access, ownership per se was not associated with greater risk of thoughts of shooting others 3.
text.formatted: Interestingly, thoughts of shooting others were not associated with current gun ownership, indicating that despite having access, ownership per se was not associated with greater risk of thoughts of shooting others <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref>.

text.text: Here, we describe the behavioral and psychological characteristics of people who report thoughts of shooting others, anticipating that its correlates would be similar to those of interpersonal firearm violence and victimization.

Specifically, because violent thoughts are associated with violent behavior 7, 8 , we examined whether thoughts of shooting others were associated with gun use either for offensive (i.e., to scare or hurt others) or defensive (i.e., to protect oneself, others, or property) purposes.
text.formatted: Specifically, because violent thoughts are associated with violent behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref> , we examined whether thoughts of shooting others were associated with gun use either for offensive (i.e., to scare or hurt others) or defensive (i.e., to protect oneself, others, or property) purposes.

text.text: We also examined associations with firearmrelated variables such as experience and engagement with firearms, storage practices, and risky behaviors such as handling or firing a gun after using drugs or alcohol, anticipating a higher risk profile.
Given the overlap between violence perpetration and victimization [9] [10] [11] , we also examined associations with firearm-and non-firearm-related victimization experiences.
text.formatted: Given the overlap between violence perpetration and victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[11]</ref> , we also examined associations with firearm-and non-firearm-related victimization experiences.

text.text: Interpersonal violence and violent victimization, in general, are associated with antisocial Characteristics Thoughts of Shooting Others 5 behavior, intimate partner violence, substance use problems, and disinhibited personality traits as well as mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts and behaviors 9, [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] .
text.formatted: Interpersonal violence and violent victimization, in general, are associated with antisocial Characteristics Thoughts of Shooting Others 5 behavior, intimate partner violence, substance use problems, and disinhibited personality traits as well as mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18]</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, we anticipated all these characteristics would be elevated among respondents endorsing thoughts of shooting others.
Data were collected as part of the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide (NFACS) survey of US adults aged 18 years or older, the details of which have been described elsewhere 19 .
text.formatted: Data were collected as part of the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide (NFACS) survey of US adults aged 18 years or older, the details of which have been described elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">19</ref> .

text.text: The survey was developed by the study team and fielded by a market research company, Verasight, from May 27 to September 2, 2025.
Participants were recruited using random address-based sampling (ABS) of the US Postal Service database or MMS/SMS text messaging from voter files and supplemental commercial records.
Response rates were 3.83% (n = 1,914) and 0.39% (n = 8,652) for the ABS and MMS/SMS text messaging, respectively.
While these rates are low, the ABS response rate is similar to that of recently recruited samples 20 , and low response rates are not necessarily indicative of nonresponse bias [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: While these rates are low, the ABS response rate is similar to that of recently recruited samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">20</ref> , and low response rates are not necessarily indicative of nonresponse bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref> .

text.text: From these responses, 2,829 (26.7%) were removed due to incomplete data and 703 (6.7%) were excluded during the quality assurance process, which included confirming all responses corresponded with a US IP address, no duplicate responses were provided, excluding nonhuman responses, and removing respondents who completed the survey in less than 30% of the median completion time.
This yielded a sample of 1,509 ABS-and 5,525 MMS/SMSrecruited participants (N = 7,034).

Raking was used to create survey weights to align the sample with national benchmarks from the July 2025 Current Population Survey for age, sex, race, ethnicity, income, education, political party identification, region, and metropolitan status.
The study was reviewed by the University of Michigan IRB and received an exempt determination.
Prior to accessing the survey, participants reviewed information on the survey content, length of the survey, and compensation, and were informed that participation was voluntary and anonymous.
All participants provided active consent prior to receiving survey questions, and all surveys were completed online.
Thoughts of Shooting Others.

Respondents rated their level of agreement with the item: "I have thought about shooting another person or multiple people." 3 A response of strongly agree, agree, or somewhat agree was coded as "Yes"; a response of strongly disagree, disagree, or somewhat disagree was coded as "No."
text.formatted: Respondents rated their level of agreement with the item: "I have thought about shooting another person or multiple people." <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref> A response of strongly agree, agree, or somewhat agree was coded as "Yes"; a response of strongly disagree, disagree, or somewhat disagree was coded as "No."

text.text: If a respondent endorsed an affirmative response, they were asked the same question for the past 12 months.
Respondents were asked: "In what ways have you used a gun to protect yourself, another person, your property, or someone else's property?"

10, 24 Respondents were given a list of possible DGU and told to select all that applied: told someone I had a gun (and I actually had a gun), showed someone that I had a gun, waved a gun around as a threat, pointed a gun at someone, fired a warning shot at someone, fired a gun at someone to shoot them but missed, shot someone.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24</ref> Respondents were given a list of possible DGU and told to select all that applied: told someone I had a gun (and I actually had a gun), showed someone that I had a gun, waved a gun around as a threat, pointed a gun at someone, fired a warning shot at someone, fired a gun at someone to shoot them but missed, shot someone.

text.text: Endorsement of any of the options was coded as lifetime DGU.
Respondents were asked: "In what ways have you used a gun not for protection or defense, but to scare, intimidate, threaten, rob, hurt, or kill someone?"
10, 24 Respondents were given a list of possible OGU that paralleled those for DGU, with additional options of using a gun to rob someone or to damage property.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24</ref> Respondents were given a list of possible OGU that paralleled those for DGU, with additional options of using a gun to rob someone or to damage property.

text.text: Endorsement of any of the options was coded as lifetime OGU.
Firearm experience.

All respondents were asked about their experience and expertise with using firearms, "Do you know how to use a gun, and have experience shooting a gun?", and how frequently they participate in firearm-related activities, "How often do you participate in activities like hunting, target shooting, work on guns (e.g., clean, repair), go to gun stores or shows, watch or listen to gun-oriented programs (e.g., podcasts, videos), visiting websites or read about guns, hunting, or shooting?"
(see Table 1 for response options).
text.formatted: (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for response options).

text.text: Firearm ownership and storage.
Respondents reported their current gun ownership status.
Current firearm owners were then asked several questions related to firearm storage, including whether their firearms were stored locked and/or loaded.

For these analyses, we compared gun owners with and without a history of having thoughts of shooting others on whether (1) at least one of their firearms was stored unlocked and (2) at least one firearm was stored unlocked and loaded.
Respondents were asked if they had ever handled a gun after drinking alcohol or using cannabis, and if they had ever fired a gun after drinking alcohol or under the influence of cannabis.
If a respondent endorsed any of these items, they were asked the same questions about the past 12 months.
Respondents were asked, separately, if they or anyone close to them (e.g., relative, friend) had ever been shot due to an act of violence.
For other forms of nonfatal firearm victimization (NFV), respondents were asked, "Has someone ever used a gun to try to scare, intimidate, threaten, rob, hurt, or kill you or someone with you?"
with response options that paralleled OGU with appropriate wording modifications (e.g., pointed a gun at me or someone I was with) 10, 24 .
text.formatted: with response options that paralleled OGU with appropriate wording modifications (e.g., pointed a gun at me or someone I was with) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24</ref> .

text.text: Endorsement of any of the options was coded as lifetime NFV.

Respondents were also asked if they had ever been the victim of other violent crimes including being stalked; threatened with a weapon; robbed; home break-in; physically attacked with or without a weapon; sexually assaulted with or without a weapon.
An affirmative response to any of these options was coded as lifetime violent victimization.

Respondents rated their level of agreement with the following item: "I have thought about using a gun to attempt suicide," using the same response options and coding as the thoughts of shooting others items 25.
text.formatted: Respondents rated their level of agreement with the following item: "I have thought about using a gun to attempt suicide," using the same response options and coding as the thoughts of shooting others items <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">25</ref>.

text.text: Eight binary items assessed nonspecific suicidal thoughts and behaviors (e.g., suicidal ideation, done something to prepare for a suicide attempt), including past suicide attempts and nonsuicidal self-harm.
A total score was calculated for lifetime ( = .88) and the past 12 months ( = .80).
Theory-based suicide risk factors.

We included markers of thoughts and feelings over the past 2 weeks to assess trait/state constructs from models of suicide risk, specifically, defeat (2 items), entrapment (2 items), thwarted belongingness (3 items), and perceived burdensomeness (4 items) 26 27,28 .
text.formatted: We included markers of thoughts and feelings over the past 2 weeks to assess trait/state constructs from models of suicide risk, specifically, defeat (2 items), entrapment (2 items), thwarted belongingness (3 items), and perceived burdensomeness (4 items) <ref type="bibr">26 27,28</ref> .

text.text: The mean of the 11 items ( = .89) served as the measure of 𝛼 proximal suicide risk factors.
We used the PHQ-2 ( = .88) 𝛼 29 and the GAD-2 ( = .87) 𝛼 30 to assess depression and generalized anxiety over the past 2 weeks, respectively.
text.formatted: We used the PHQ-2 ( = .88) 𝛼 <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">29</ref> and the GAD-2 ( = .87) 𝛼 <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">30</ref> to assess depression and generalized anxiety over the past 2 weeks, respectively.

text.text: Drug and alcohol use.
Lifetime and past 12-month alcohol, nicotine, and drug use were assessed using the Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test 31 .
text.formatted: Lifetime and past 12-month alcohol, nicotine, and drug use were assessed using the Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">31</ref> .

text.text: Negative consequences of alcohol and cannabis use were assessed using items adapted from the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test 32 and Cannabis Use Disorder Identification Test-Revised 33 , respectively, with some additions including items that assessed lifetime and past 12month problem use.
text.formatted: Negative consequences of alcohol and cannabis use were assessed using items adapted from the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">32</ref> and Cannabis Use Disorder Identification Test-Revised <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">33</ref> , respectively, with some additions including items that assessed lifetime and past 12month problem use.

text.text: Respondents completed seven items that asked how many times Characteristics Thoughts of Shooting Others 9 (never, once or twice, several times, many times) they had engaged in various types of antisocial behavior including theft, destroying property, lying and conning, and aggression and violence, as well as being arrested and suspended or expelled from school ( = .79).
Respondents were asked whether they ever had a romantic relationship with the same partner that lasted longer than 1 month.

Eligible respondents (n = 6372) completed 5 items adapted from the Controlling and Abusive Tactics-2 34 and Conflict Tactics Scale-2 35 that asked how frequently (never, rare, occasional, common, frequent) they attempt to control who their current or most recent romantic partner spends time with; search their partner's purse, wallet, or cell phone; threaten to hurt their partner; push, slap, hit, kick, punch, or choke their partner; or use a knife, gun, or other weapon on their partner ( = .63).
text.formatted: Eligible respondents (n = 6372) completed 5 items adapted from the Controlling and Abusive Tactics-2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">34</ref> and Conflict Tactics Scale-2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">35</ref> that asked how frequently (never, rare, occasional, common, frequent) they attempt to control who their current or most recent romantic partner spends time with; search their partner's purse, wallet, or cell phone; threaten to hurt their partner; push, slap, hit, kick, punch, or choke their partner; or use a knife, gun, or other weapon on their partner ( = .63).

text.text: Respondents were also asked whether they had ever been the victim of the same behaviors by their intimate partner ( = .84).

We included markers of several personality traits including antagonism versus agreeableness (3 items, = .72) and conscientiousness (4 items, = .62) 𝛼 𝛼 ; negative urgency (4 items, = .83) 𝛼 ; persecutory ideas (3 items, = .72); desire for power (3 items, = 𝛼 𝛼 .71) and feeling powerless (3 items, = .72) 𝛼 ; subjective well-being (4 items, = .84) 𝛼 .

Survey-weighted logistic and linear regression models were fit to compare respondents who endorsed thoughts of shooting others in the past 12 months and lifetime with respondents who did not on the various firearm, psychological, and behavioral measures.
We fit unadjusted models and adjusted models that included the covariates of age, sex, race/ethnicity, income, and education.
Standard errors were estimated using Taylor-series linearization.
There was no missing data.
All analyses were conducted in Stata 19 using the Survey data analysis module.
pattern of effect sizes and confidence intervals across measures rather than on the significance of any specific measure and did not adjust p-values for multiple comparisons.
When summarizing the results, we report the mean of the unadjusted and adjusted ORs for the variable being discussed unless otherwise noted.

For quantitative variables, differences between respondents who did versus did not report thoughts of shooting others were expressed in standard deviation (SD) units by dividing the mean difference by the pooled SD.
Firearm-related variables.

Associations were similar for thoughts of shooting others in the past 12 months and lifetime reporting periods; therefore, we are referring to both time frames when describing associations with thoughts of shooting others unless otherwise noted.
Respondents who self-reported OGU (mean OR = 3.41) and DGU (mean OR = 3.38) had higher odds of thoughts of shooting others (Table 1).
text.formatted: Respondents who self-reported OGU (mean OR = 3.41) and DGU (mean OR = 3.38) had higher odds of thoughts of shooting others (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Respondents with more experience and expertise with firearms also had higher odds of endorsing thoughts of shooting others (mean OR = 2.17), as did those who participated in more firearm-related activities (mean OR = 1.71).

Current gun owners who stored at least one firearm unlocked had higher odds of endorsing thoughts of shooting others (mean OR = 2.78), as did gun owners who stored at least one firearm unlocked and loaded (mean OR = 3.11).

Respondents who reported handling or firing a gun after drinking alcohol or under the influence of cannabis had much higher odds of reporting thoughts of shooting others than those who did not (mean OR = 4.73).
Respondents who were shot due to violence (mean OR = 4.94) or had a relative or friend shot due to violence (mean OR = 1.95) had higher odds of lifetime thoughts of shooting others (Table 2).
text.formatted: Respondents who were shot due to violence (mean OR = 4.94) or had a relative or friend shot due to violence (mean OR = 1.95) had higher odds of lifetime thoughts of shooting others (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Respondents who reported NFV (mean OR = 2.24) and other types of violent victimization (mean OR = 2.64) also had higher odds of reporting thoughts of shooting others.
Thoughts of firearm suicide, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and mental health problems.
Thoughts of firearm suicide had a large association with thoughts of shooting others (mean OR = 7.28).

Table 3 reports the unstandardized regression coefficients estimating mean differences in suicide and mental health outcomes between respondents who did or did not endorse thoughts of shooting others.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> reports the unstandardized regression coefficients estimating mean differences in suicide and mental health outcomes between respondents who did or did not endorse thoughts of shooting others.

text.text: Respondents endorsing thoughts of shooting others had higher mean levels of lifetime and past 12-month suicidal thoughts and behaviors (about 0.75 and 0.50 SD units, respectively) and proximal risk factors for suicide (mean 0.68 SD units) (Table 3).
text.formatted: Respondents endorsing thoughts of shooting others had higher mean levels of lifetime and past 12-month suicidal thoughts and behaviors (about 0.75 and 0.50 SD units, respectively) and proximal risk factors for suicide (mean 0.68 SD units) (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Thoughts of shooting others were also associated with higher mean levels of depression and generalized anxiety in the past two weeks (mean 0.49 SDs).

Respondents who reported thoughts of shooting others also reported using a greater variety of drugs as well as more alcohol and cannabis userelated problems for their lifetime and in the past 12 months (mean 0.34 SD units) (Table 4).
text.formatted: Respondents who reported thoughts of shooting others also reported using a greater variety of drugs as well as more alcohol and cannabis userelated problems for their lifetime and in the past 12 months (mean 0.34 SD units) (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Respondents who reported thoughts of shooting others reported higher mean levels of antisocial behavior (mean 0.97 SD units) and IPV as both an aggressor and victim (mean 0.59 SD units).

Thoughts of shooting others were associated with higher scores on antagonism (mean 0.87 SD units), persecutory ideas (mean 0.87 SD units), negative urgency (mean 0.69 SD units), desire for power (mean 0.54 SD units), and feeling powerless (mean 0.54 SD units).
Thoughts of shooting others were also associated with lower scores on conscientiousness (mean -0.61 SD units) and subjective well-being (mean -0.57 SD units).

We examined the characteristics associated with having thoughts of shooting others, and found a complex risk profile spanning firearm behaviors, victimization experiences, mental Characteristics Thoughts of Shooting Others 12 health and substance use problems, antisocial behavior, and disinhibited personality traits.

These characteristics were consistent with the correlates of interpersonal violence and victimization 9, [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] , which suggests that assessing thoughts of shooting others may be effective in identifying a high-risk group for firearm violence.
text.formatted: These characteristics were consistent with the correlates of interpersonal violence and victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18]</ref> , which suggests that assessing thoughts of shooting others may be effective in identifying a high-risk group for firearm violence.

text.text: This was further supported by higher rates of self-reported OGU and DGU among those who reported thoughts of shooting others, indicating that for a subset of respondents, these thoughts are associated with actions, though the temporal ordering could not be determined.

One of the strongest correlates of thoughts of shooting others was thoughts of suicide by firearm, consistent with a close association between interpersonal and self-directed violence 16, 17 and a sign that people having these thoughts experience significant psychiatric distress.
text.formatted: One of the strongest correlates of thoughts of shooting others was thoughts of suicide by firearm, consistent with a close association between interpersonal and self-directed violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">17</ref> and a sign that people having these thoughts experience significant psychiatric distress.

text.text: This interpretation is supported by the elevated levels of non-specific suicidal thoughts and behaviors, depression, anxiety, and firearm-and non-firearm-related victimization experiences among those reporting thoughts of shooting others.
It is possible these victimization experiences are a common risk factor for psychiatric symptoms and thoughts of firearm homicide and suicide.
Thoughts of shooting others were also associated with high levels of antisocial behavior, substance use problems, and disinhibited personality traits.
These disinhibited behaviors may increase risk of exposure to situations in which victimization is more likely 9, 40, 41.
text.formatted: These disinhibited behaviors may increase risk of exposure to situations in which victimization is more likely <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">41</ref>.

text.text: Further, a personality structure characterized by antagonism, beliefs that others have malevolent intentions, impulsivity, a desire to control others, but feelings of a lack of agency, happiness, and satisfaction in their life could be both risk factors for and the consequence of victimization and thoughts of shooting others.
Unfortunately, the cross-sectional design does not allow us to delineate what are likely bidirectional influences among these variables.

Our prior analysis showed that thoughts of shooting others were not associated with current gun ownership, but here we found they were associated with greater experience and engagement with firearms, as well as with insecure firearm storage (e.g., unlocked and loaded)
Characteristics Thoughts of Shooting Others 13 and with handling or firing a gun while under the influence of alcohol and cannabis.
Again, the temporal direction of these associations could not be determined, i.e., whether greater firearm exposure preceded thoughts of shooting others or vice versa.

It is also possible that characteristics such as behavioral disinhibition and psychiatric problems are common risk factors for thoughts of shooting others, insecure storage, and risky firearm behaviors generally.
Limitations included the cross-sectional design, which did not allow for inferences about causal influences underlying the numerous correlates.

Also, we did not assess the context of thoughts of shooting others, for example, whether for offensive or defensive purposes, or whether they were reactive or premeditated, and other features such as frequency and duration.
Completing the survey required online access and English proficiency, and respondents may have interpreted certain questions differently.

The response rate was low, and while the survey weights aligned certain sample characteristics to population benchmarks, they did not correct for any potential nonresponse bias on unmeasured characteristics.

Numerous behavioral and psychological factors were associated with thoughts of shooting others, which may help identify a group with an elevated risk profile for firearm violence, though imminent danger should not be inferred from thoughts alone 42 .
text.formatted: Numerous behavioral and psychological factors were associated with thoughts of shooting others, which may help identify a group with an elevated risk profile for firearm violence, though imminent danger should not be inferred from thoughts alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">42</ref> .

text.text: The complexity of these correlates suggests a variety of risk processes-some of which likely overlap-that should be considered when conceptualizing prevention and intervention efforts for firearm violence and victimization.
